articles.title: Newsom moves to commute all California death sentences to life in prison without parole
articles.summary: The outgoing governor's plan to remove the threat of capital punishment hanging over more than 500 condemned inmates comes as he considers a run for presiden...
articles.body:
Gov. Gavin Newsom told the California Supreme Court on Thursday that he will commute the death sentences of all 548 state prisoners awaiting execution, reducing their punishments to life in prison without parole.

Newsom can commute about 40% of the death sentences with the stroke of a pen, but the rest will require the high court's approval in order to be finalized.

The mass commutation would apply to men and women convicted of some of the most heinous acts in the state's history. Newsom and other opponents of capital punishment have long argued that the process is costly, cruel and discriminatory, with death sentences disproportionately handed down to defendants of color.

"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundation of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom wrote in a letter to Californians explaining his decision . "I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency."

The move comes in Newsom's final months as governor and as he considers a run for president. Reducing the death sentences could help him in a primary with a Democratic base of like-minded liberal voters, but potentially hurt him in a general election with a national electorate that supports capital punishment.

The decision to officially spare the condemned inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs every year. Only 13 inmates have been killed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978. The state's electorate reaffirmed its support a decade ago, voting down a ballot initiative that would have abolished capital punishment. Polls show its popularity has waned in the years since.

Despite his outspoken opposition to state-sanctioned executions, the governor has declined to use his political influence with voters to pursue a ballot measure that would amend the state Constitution to align with his position and officially end the death penalty. Without changing state law, criminals can continue to be sentenced to death in California.

"California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books and I respect that," Newsom wrote in the letter to Californians. "But the Constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment."

Newsom made national headlines two months after his inauguration in 2019 when he issued a temporary moratorium on executions and vowed to dismantle the death chamber at San Quentin State Prison, now called San Quentin Rehabilitation Center.

Calling the death penalty system a "failure," Newsom said the punishment is also often reserved for poor people who cannot afford expensive legal representation, fails to deter crime and wastes taxpayer money.

Careful to avoid elevating a death penalty debate in the midterm elections, Newsom intentionally waited until after the general election on Tuesday to go a step further and launch the process of commuting all California death penalty sentences.

The decision is another bold signature Newsom move that sits well with his base of support in California and wealthy, white and college-educated national voters who would be crucial to his success in a Democratic presidential primary, said Mike Madrid, a Republican political consultant.

"Gavin's exactly right with that base Democratic voter on that position," Madrid said. "One hundred percent. It makes him a champion."

However, his liberal stance on government executions could also create a vulnerability for him if he advances in the 2028 presidential election as the party's nominee. More moderate blue-collar voters who helped the party flip Congress in the midterms, Madrid added, are "not in line with him on this."

A poll conducted in August by the Pew Research Center found that about two-thirds of voters nationally favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder.

Those numbers could shift following the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's now-scuttled plan to livestream the execution of Ft. Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad.

"Those events have really ripped the veneer off the death penalty in this country," said attorney Natasha Minsker of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition. "The death penalty is an act of violence. It's taking another life. I think that's become clear to the entire country."

The state spends more than $200 million a year to adjudicate automatic death penalty appeals and habeas corpus petitions for inmates who, in all likelihood, will never be executed, according to a 2025 report by the Habeas Corpus Resource Center.

The case of Clarence Ray Allen, the last inmate killed by lethal injection in California 20 years ago, is emblematic of how the law has failed, death penalty opponents say.

Allen was 76, making him the second-oldest person ever executed in the United States. He had been on death row for 23 years and his appeals cost the state more than $750,000. Many current condemned inmates are even older — some in their 80s and 90s — and their appeals even more drawn-out and expensive.

"It's just a broken system," said Michael Hersek, former executive director of Habeas Corpus Resource Center and an ex-state public defender.

Taxpayers foot the bill for both the defense and the prosecution in post-conviction capital cases, as well as the administrative judicial costs associated with years of complicated appeals in state and federal court.

The existing appeal requirements were instituted to counter long-standing racial bias in capital sentencing. Attempts to reform and expedite the appeals process over the years have further gummed up the system.

"There is no indication that the situation has improved, and ... [there are] data indicating that it has worsened," Justice Leondra R. Kruger wrote for the California Supreme Court in 2024.

It's estimated that death penalty appeals alone constitute about a quarter of the work of the California Supreme Court.

"It's ludicrous, the amount of time, resources and energy put into these cases," Hersek said.

"The death penalty is this promise to people who are angry and broken that you're somehow going to make them feel better by executing this person," said Bethany Webb , whose sister Laura was among eight people killed in a mass shooting in Seal Beach in 2011.

Their mother was also badly injured in the attack.

"It is brutalizing to family members, the whole system," Webb said.

More joined the chorus in the wake of the announcement.

"The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn't. It's a distraction from what we actually need," said Jess Nichol, whose 12-year-old sister, Polly Klaas, was abducted from their Petaluma home and murdered in 1993, sparking a search that gripped the nation.

Others say Newsom's latest move is a betrayal of the justice they were promised.

"It's total disrespect for the victims. It's a slap in the face," said Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son, Michael Lyons, was abducted, raped and murdered in 1996.

She and other relatives stressed the unique brutality of many capital crimes, saying Newsom did not consider victims' suffering when commuting their killers' sentences.

"[Newsom] has a heart for criminals, I don't think he has a heart for victims," said Phyllis Loya, whose son, Larry Lasater, a police officer in Pittsburg, Calif., was killed in the line of duty by a man who was sentenced to death. "He doesn't care about us."

The commutations would go to inmates such as Charles Ng, who was convicted of killing six men, three women and two infant boys in Northern California in 1984 and 1985. Also in line to benefit is Klaas' killer, Richard Allen Davis, who famously flipped cameras the bird after he was convicted. Another condemned inmate, Christopher Cheary, was convicted of murdering, raping and torturing his girlfriend's 3-year-old daughter, Sophia Acosta, in Tulare County.

Former Sacramento County Dist. Atty. Anne Marie Schubert, the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation and a death penalty supporter, said the families of murder victims had been "run over, torn up, and thrown in the garbage" by the commutations.

The governor decided that his personal opinion was more important than judges, juries and the will of the voters, she said, questioning why Newsom didn't take action when he first took office instead of enacting a blanket reprieve on his way out as governor.

"It is perhaps the greatest travesty of justice I've ever witnessed," Schubert said. "I think what's particularly concerning is that the families of murdered children, killed police officers and [victims of] school shooters, mass shooters and baby killers — those families were not even given the decency of a phone call or a meeting or any kind of notice."

Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra also opposes the death penalty. If state leaders wanted to resume executions, experts say it would take the better part of a decade and millions of dollars in new spending for the state to design and approve a workable protocol for lethal injections, rebuild a death chamber and secure the gray-market drugs necessary to perform executions.

Legal experts believe the end of the death penalty is likely inevitable in California, with or without Newsom's involvement.

In 2024, the Office of the State Public Defender sued California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta's office, arguing "persistent and pervasive racial disparities infect California's death penalty system."

This spring, the California Supreme Court ordered Bonta's California Department of Justice to show cause why it should not declare the death penalty unconstitutional — a move widely read as signaling the justices' ultimate intent to end it.

"The statistical findings in the studies invoked by petitioners are extraordinarily disturbing," Bonta wrote in his reply to the order in August. "Evidence of pervasive racial disparities in the administration of the death penalty could show that California's capital punishment system gives rise to a constitutionally intolerable risk of arbitrariness."

Among the 529 men and 19 women in line for commutations, around 60% would require review and approval by the California Supreme Court before Newsom's term ends in January. Those cases involve prisoners who had a felony conviction on their record prior to receiving a death sentence, or racked up additional crimes while awaiting execution.

The high court previously rejected 10 clemency cases without much clarification when Gov. Jerry Brown submitted them in 2018 months before he left office.

If the mass commutation is approved by the California Supreme Court, the immediate effect could be relatively muted. The death chamber was taken down and all but a handful of the remaining condemned inmates were relocated from segregated housing in San Quentin to other facilities across the state after Newsom's 2019 moratorium.

The decision to formally pause executions drew support from the late Pope Francis during Newsom's 2024 trip to the Vatican, according to the governor's retelling of a brief conversation between the two men.

In a subsequent interview, the governor said his Catholic background and the inequities in the criminal justice system influenced his refusal to sign off on executions. His father, the late William Newsom, also opposed the death penalty.

His father and grandfather were involved in the case of Pete Pianezzi, a friend who was wrongfully convicted of first-degree murder in the shooting and killing of a gambler and busboy in Los Angeles in 1937.

Pianezzi escaped the death penalty by a single vote and served 13 years in prison. He was later exonerated.

Even if it were possible to limit inequity and wrongful convictions in the criminal justice system, Newsom has said he would still be against the death penalty.

"The decision is among the most difficult in my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims' families," Newsom wrote in the letter to Californians. "Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing."

California politics editor Phil Willon contributed reporting.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Melania Trump calls for peace at meeting with Russia, Ukraine officials
articles.summary: US first lady hosts Russian, Ukrainian officials at the White House, urges two sides to build on recent local truce.
articles.body:
United States First Lady Melania Trump has urged Russia and Ukraine to build on a recent localised ceasefire and seek a more “enduring” peace, as she hosted officials from both countries at the White House.

Melania Trump spoke on Thursday at an event that the White House said is believed to be “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.

Those attending included Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy of Russian President Vladimir Putin; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.

“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” Mrs. Trump said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.

She said her role as “exclusive intermediary” was set out in written agreements signed by both countries, and that she was involved in every stage of the planning, including reviewing de-mining plans and evacuation routes.

Ukrainian representatives presented the US first lady with the Order of Princess Olga, first class, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded her earlier this week. She also gave the most senior officials present letters she had written to Putin and Zelenskyy.

The six-day truce covered the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region and the surrounding area, and allowed aid deliveries and the evacuation of nearly 800 people.

An estimated 2,000 civilians had been left in the city. It was the longest multi-day truce between Russia and Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the first joint relief operation in four years and eight months.

The White House said Melania Trump mediated the truce, though Pope Leo XIV also pressed both sides to allow aid and evacuations, and that the two accounts of who brokered it have diverged.

The truce expired last Sunday with no extension, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region, killed at least 40 people, according to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy.

New US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.

articles.summary: House GOP leadership letter from Steve Scalise warns committee chairs to prepare defenses against expected Democrat-led probes of Trump allies.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: House GOP leadership is giving Republican lawmakers a new playbook to go up against an expected barrage of Democrat-led investigations in the new Congress. Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., wrote a letter to the current chairs of House committees on Thursday warning them to "maximize our remaining days in power to prepare for what is coming" with instructions on how to brace for those expected probes. A source sent a copy of that letter to Fox News Digital. "House Democrats have signaled they intend to impeach President Trump, but they will not stop there. They will weaponize every single gavel to appease their radical base," Scalise said. "They will use their oversight authorities to harass the President, his family, cabinet officials, and they will seek to destroy our allies. You all will be a key line of defense in this fight." The guidance includes three key points: "taking inventory" of current and likely future investigative efforts by Democrats while they are in the minority, identifying who is on Democrats' target list, and reviewing how recent Supreme Court rulings as well as a Department of Justice (DOJ) memo on executive privilege could factor into future investigations. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMOCRATS, REPUBLICANS WASTE NO TIME IN SETTING SOCIAL MEDIA ABLAZE AFTER MIDTERM SWEEP Democrats' targets could include "administration officials, programs and authorities, and external allies, including conservative partners and industry leaders," Scalise said. He added that his staff would meet with the relevant committees and others to further prepare. "Please let me know if there are any additional tools or support you need from me as you undertake this important effort," Scalise wrote. "I have full confidence that we will be effective in our efforts to fight back as a team." Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the likely next head of the House Oversight Committee, released a brief statement Tuesday night when it was projected Democrats would win the House: "Lawyer up." Scalise is asking his fellow Republicans to compile a list of all the corruption, lawlessness, and abuse they’ve been protecting from congressional oversight. But the people have spoken, and the cover-up expires with the Republican majority. The days of invertebrate congressional submission are over." The letter comes a day after Scalise launched a bid to become House minority leader in the new Congress. He will be up against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, for the job. articles.title: Crenshaw, Raskin shout each other down in heated post-midterm debate
articles.summary: Texas Republican Rep. Dan Crenshaw and Democratic Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin clashed in a fiery CNN exchange on Wednesday after the midterm elections.
articles.body:
Rep. Dan Crenshaw, R-Texas, and Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., engaged in a heated exchange on CNN Wednesday over the results of the midterm elections .

The midterm elections dealt a major setback to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party as Democrats retook control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, while also winning several key gubernatorial races, including Texas, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Though Raskin celebrated the Democrats' victories as a way to help the American people, Crenshaw argued that Senate Democrats had refused to pass widely supported legislation ahead of the elections. He pointed to the Stop Insider Trading Act as an example and said Trump would likely sign it if the bill reached his desk, prompting Raskin to criticize the administration.

"You think he would?" Raskin remarked. "Let's mark that down. Because their whole administration is about insider trading."

"You're missing the point," Crenshaw replied.

"No, you're missing the point. And you guys lost the election because you missed the point," Raskin said.

Crenshaw accused Democrats of refusing to pass legislation in an effort to make Republicans look bad ahead of the election. Although Raskin and CNN host Dana Bash noted during the segment that Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress and the White House, Crenshaw repeatedly reminded Raskin that most legislation requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster in the Senate, more than Republicans held before the election.

Raskin, however, accused Crenshaw and Senate Republicans of covering for Trump.

"You guys didn't want to pass anything, you just wanted to support Donald Trump's corruption!" Raskin exclaimed.

"What does that even mean? Stop talking!" Crenshaw said.

"Well, it means something to the American people! Look at the election results!" Raskin said.

"Are you capable of doing anything but talking just in talking points? Do you actually have facts? I'm reading bills. I'm doing actual policy discussions. You're just yelling. Are you confused?" Crenshaw said.

Crenshaw continued to mock Raskin for claiming the Democratic Party could tackle affordability, pointing out that Democrats still had not secured 60 votes in the Senate after the midterm elections.

"Tell me, how you're gonna do affordability? How are you gonna do that?" Crenshaw said.

"Well, we're going to start by getting rid of your illegal tariffs. That's the first thing which have driven up prices. Then we're going to try to end your illegal war —" Raskin said.

"Again, civics lesson: you can't pass laws. You don't have 60 votes in the Senate. So, how do I need to remind you of that?" Crenshaw said.

The two continued to argue until Bash intervened, saying she appreciated hearing a debate about policy issues.

"As heated as this has gotten, I have to say it is actually nice to hear the debate of issues and ideas, because we don't hear that enough," Bash said.

White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told Fox News Digital, "Under President Trump's leadership, this administration has signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, and locked in nearly 20 trade deals."

"Moving forward, the President will work with anyone willing to advance solutions that strengthen our economy and put more money back in the pockets of American workers," he added. "We hope Democrats will put the American people first and join us in that effort."

"Raskin loves seeing himself on camera," Republican commentator Matt Gorman told Fox News Digital. "He's a hypocrite of the first order and this exchange exposed it."

Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Crenshaw and Raskin for comment but did not immediately receive responses.

articles.title: Dunlap concedes to LePage in Maine battleground
articles.summary: The former Republican governor is poised to flip Jared Golden’s seat in what could be the GOP’s only House pickup outside of redistricting.
articles.body:
Former Gov. Paul LePage declared victory Thursday in Maine's 2nd District as Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded, giving Republicans their first and possibly only pickup in the House that wasn't a result of GOP redistricting.

The seat, which was open because of the retirement of incumbent Rep. Jared Golden (D), ends a Democratic grip on a deep-red district carried twice by President Donald Trump.

Dunlap's campaign said the race was headed to a ranked-choice count but that it did not expect the process to change the outcome.

"This isn't the result we were hoping for, and I'm disappointed that we came short," the candidate said in a statement. "Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best."

LePage adviser Brent Littlefield said blank ballots and write-ins could trigger the statutory ranked-choice process but that the Republican had a decisive advantage of more than 4,400 votes.

"It is very clear from our campaign team's work yesterday talking one-on-one with many local town clerks and the publicly reported numbers that Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect," Littlefield said in a statement.

Dunlap, Maine's state auditor and a former secretary of state, originally entered the race to challenge Golden from the left, accusing him of voting too often with Republicans. But the incumbent instead announced his retirement , citing increasing political incivility and the toll of public service on his family.

National Democrats initially backed state Sen. Joe Baldacci in the primary, but Dunlap prevailed in a ranked-choice runoff. Dunlap had support from the Bernie Sanders-linked Our Revolution and benefited from more than $500,000 in spending by an outside group with apparent GOP ties that boosted him and attacked Baldacci.

LePage, a former two-term governor, entered the contest with an established base in the district.

He now looks forward to working with "anyone — and everyone — regardless of Party to put Maine first," Littlefield said.

articles.title: Hegseth demands $350B for military, fires back at Dem impeachment push
articles.summary: War Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress to approve $350 billion in military funding and vowed to fight Democratic impeachment efforts.
articles.body: War Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress Thursday to approve at least $350 billion in defense funding while pushing back against efforts to impeach him. In a video posted to X, Hegseth defended his Pentagon overhaul, including eliminating DEI initiatives, removing military leaders and rebuilding recruitment. Hegseth dismissed the impeachment push as political theater while defending his efforts to overhaul the Pentagon and advance President Donald Trump's military agenda. HEGSETH FACES BIPARTISAN IMPEACHMENT THREAT AFTER IRAN WAR GETS BLAME FOR GOP MIDTERM SLAUGHTER "We need every vote from every patriotic member of Congress," Hegseth said, calling for a reconciliation bill of at least $350 billion to strengthen the military and defense industrial base. The impeachment effort is being led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who introduced eight articles against Hegseth in September, accusing him of violating congressional war powers during the Iran conflict and abusing his authority in other military operations. Massie, who lost his Republican primary in May, plans to renew the effort when Congress returns next week. The House has not voted on the articles. Trump defended Hegseth on Thursday, telling ABC News he intends to keep him in his Cabinet despite the impeachment push. GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH Hegseth dismissed the effort as politically motivated. "A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly," Hegseth said. He also took aim at former President Joe Biden and former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, accusing them of leaving the Pentagon in disarray and forcing the Trump administration to rebuild the military. "We ended the weird and the woke and elevated patriots in strength," Hegseth said, defending his efforts to eliminate diversity initiatives and change military personnel policies. HEGSETH'S LEADERSHIP QUESTIONED BY GOP MILITARY VETERAN AS DEMOCRATS TALK IMPEACHMENT Hegseth also defended the administration's military operations against Iran, describing the campaign as a historic effort to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. articles.title: Democrats ‘divorced from voters’ as 5 states back citizen-only voting, bolstering GOP push
articles.summary: Voters in Kansas, Alaska, Arkansas, South Dakota and West Virginia approved noncitizen voting bans by wide margins, but a key Supreme Court case looms.
articles.body: Voters in five states overwhelmingly approved ballot measures barring noncitizens from voting, including Kansas, where Democrats scored a major Senate upset, and Alaska, where the Senate race remains uncalled. Federal law already prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, but measures approved in Kansas, Alaska, Arkansas, South Dakota and West Virginia clarify or explicitly codify citizenship requirements for voting in state and local elections, with support exceeding 60% in each state. Election integrity advocates pointed to the results as evidence supporting President Donald Trump and Republicans’ argument that their push to require proof of citizenship for federal voter registration has "overwhelming bipartisan support." REPUBLICANS SUFFER HISTORIC SENATE UPSET AS DEM FLIPS DEEP-RED STATE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY A CENTURY "I would absolutely agree that noncitizen voting bans are overwhelmingly popular," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, told Fox News Digital. "They enjoy bipartisan support." A 2024 Gallup poll found that 83% of Americans, including 66% of Democrats, support requiring first-time voters to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote. The ballot measure wins also come as the conservative-majority Supreme Court prepares to consider a related dispute over whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship on its state voter registration form and remove suspected noncitizens from the rolls before an election, a ruling that could affect how states enforce citizenship requirements. Related election measures failed in California and Arizona. California’s Proposition 39 was defeated 58.5% to 41.4%, a margin of roughly 17 percentage points; the measure would have required voter ID and additional citizenship-verification procedures. "I would note that the unique thing there is not only that California is openly hostile to the idea of trying to prevent noncitizen voting in terms of its elected leadership, but also the left poured more than $30 million into the ballot measure campaign to defeat that," Snead told Fox News Digital. Snead said Arizona’s measure was broader legislation that included several provisions beyond noncitizen voting, which may have contributed to its defeat. The victories for the measures barring noncitizens from voting follow the Trump administration and congressional Republicans’ failed efforts to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote. ARIZONA VOTER LAW FIGHT REACHES SCOTUS AS ELECTION GROUPS WARN ‘ABSURD’ CONSEQUENCE COULD ENSUE The SAVE America Act also became a flashpoint in Congress, with Republicans and Democrats sparring over whether to attach it to a budget reconciliation package. Trump’s effort to tie the bill to Department of Homeland Security funding contributed to a prolonged standoff during the department’s shutdown. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans lacked the votes to pass it, while Democrats argued it would disenfranchise eligible voters. Hans von Spakovsky, a former member of the Federal Election Commission and senior legal fellow of Advancing American Freedom, said the Democratic Party is completely "divorced" from its voters. Snead agreed, saying Democrats took a "90-10 issue" and turned it into a highly politicized fight. "The left is far out of step with the American public, and they really should be answering the question, 'Why are you opposed to something that 90% of the public is in favor of?" Snead said. "Only citizens should vote in our elections. And if you believe, as the left claims to, in democracy, well then, we should start by making sure that we have free and fair elections that are decided only by American citizens." But while Spakovsky applauded the passage of the ballot measures, he warned they could prove ineffective unless states are allowed to verify voters’ citizenship. "Look, I'm glad those states passed that referendum, but those provisions aren't going to be much good unless states are able to do two things," Spakovsky said. Spakovsky pointed to Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, a case in which the Supreme Court will decide whether federal law prevents Arizona from requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and from removing suspected noncitizens from its voter rolls. He said the ruling could affect how effectively states can enforce citizenship requirements. ELECTION EXPERT SOUNDS ALARM ON HOW NONCITIZENS ARE LANDING ON VOTER ROLLS Snead said simply checking a box attesting to citizenship on a federal form has not been sufficient. "As we have seen in a number of recent arrests by the Justice Department, with indictments going out against noncitizens, and with the failures of the automatic voter registration system in New Jersey, which added 6,600 noncitizens to the rolls, with almost 400 of them voting, we clearly have been let down by that check-a-box system," Snead said. However, Spakovsky said a ruling in favor of Arizona would only go so far, arguing that proof of citizenship would only apply to future voter registrations. "The only way for them to try to check the citizenship of people who are already registered is by using the SAVE database at the Department of Homeland Security, and with complete control of Congress, I have no doubt that one of the first things Democrats will do is try to defund the database so that states can't use it," Spakovsky said. Snead applauded the Trump administration's efforts to expand states’ access to the SAVE database to clean up their voter rolls, arguing the previous process of tracking down ineligible voters was "cumbersome." He also voiced concerns that Democrats will gut the database. "I think that's the direction that we are going."

articles.title: Gavin Newsom wipes out California's death row in historic mass commutation
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom will commute all 548 death sentences to life without parole, drawing sharp backlash from victims' rights advocates.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he will spare the lives of 548 inmates currently on the state’s death row, effectively clearing capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions. In a letter to constituents, Newsom, a Democrat, declared the state's capital punishment system fundamentally flawed, error-prone, and morally incompatible with California’s core values. "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom wrote. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us." EX-CHIEF SAYS CHRISTA PIKE WAS 'ALMOST GIDDY' DESCRIBING MURDER AS GOVERNOR WEIGHS IN AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION Under the executive action, all death sentences will be converted to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. The move comes amid renewed national conversations surrounding capital punishment following a botched execution in Tennessee involving death row inmate Christa Pike. California has not carried out an execution since 2006. Shortly after taking office in 2019, Newsom placed an official moratorium on executions and ordered the dismantling of the execution chamber at San Quentin State Prison. The decision drew immediate criticism from victims' rights advocates, including Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter, Polly, was kidnapped and murdered in 1993. Her killer, Richard Allen Davis, remains on death row. CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON "He just gave the gift of life to [hundreds of] people who took the gift of life from their victims," Klaas told Fox News Digital, expressing disappointment over the decision. "I don't understand his rationale behind it… but it's probably the same old tired stuff that he said when he did his moratorium." "He has definitely secured the serial killer vote now," he added. POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION Conversely, anti-death penalty advocates strongly praised the move. "The silence after the very breath of a human is violently wrestled out of them is deafening," Rev. Jeff Hood, a spiritual adviser to death row inmates, said in a statement reported by The Sacramento Bee. "I’ve heard it 14 times. Today, Governor Newsom has courageously chosen to break that silence. These commutations represent the height of moral leadership," he added. "Cruelty laid down. Now, I’m left with one prayer: God, don’t let any of the governors in the other executing states get any sleep until they find the ethical stamina to follow Newsom’s lead." Despite the move, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman noted that it doesn't eliminate the death penalty. "Only the Legislature or the voters can do that," he said in a statement. "Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes." "Until the law is changed, my office will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand. As always, we will be guided by the facts, the law and the evidence. If the Legislature or the voters remove the death penalty, we will follow that law just as faithfully," he added, noting that his thoughts "are with the families of victims, who deserve a justice system that honors the law as it is written and pursues it with fairness and due process." Dan Dow, the district attorney for San Luis Obispo County, said framed Newsom's order as an insult to murder victims. "Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California's 548 condemned killers that the killers' lives matter more," he said. "Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor tried to erase it all with a pen. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP California voters have consistently supported the death penalty. In 2016, voters rejected Proposition 62, which sought to repeal the death penalty, while narrowly approving Proposition 66 to expedite the appeals process.

articles.title: Trump stands by Hegseth after election losses, but other Republicans want him out
articles.summary: The U.S. defense secretary is facing intense political backlash over the costly and unpopular war with Iran, which the president acknowledged was partly to b...
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran following the historic drubbing Republicans took from Democrats in this week's midterm elections. But President Trump insisted on Wednesday that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief — at least not yet.

"No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters.

The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor this week.

"I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat.

According to CBS News , though, Trump "has been asking advisers" whether Hegseth should stay or go.

Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices.

Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vice President JD Vance was unequivocal.

"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war."

The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning."

"He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress."

Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him.

"I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it."

When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list.

"In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month .

Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky and vocal Trump critic, said he intends to force a House vote on articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as next week, citing violations of the War Powers Resolution, bypassing Congress on war declarations and unlawful military actions in several countries.

Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the Republican primary — introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote.

In a post on X Wednesday , Massie wrote that "there is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns."

In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to his X account on Thursday afternoon, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me."

articles.title: Ex-Alaska lawmaker details mystery recruiter as FBI, Congress widen 'Decoy Dan' scrutiny
articles.summary: The FBI interviewed former Alaska Republican David Eastman after a Democratic operative allegedly posed as a conservative recruiter in the Senate race.
articles.body: A former Alaska Republican lawmaker told Fox News Digital the FBI interviewed him after an apparent Democratic political operative allegedly posed as a conservative recruiter and tried to persuade him to enter the state's U.S. Senate race amid an intensifying congressional investigation into the controversial "Decoy Dan Sullivan" ballot scheme. The allegations raise questions about potential federal criminal liability. Article III Project attorney Will Chamberlain argued that a coordinated effort to deceive voters about a candidate's identity could violate 18 U.S.C. § 241, the federal conspiracy-against-rights statute. The revelations come after former campaign staff for Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola spoke to the New York Times about their knowledge of a reported scheme to stack Alaska’s four-person ballot with other "Dan Sullivans" to help siphon votes from incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT The ballot ultimately included Peltola, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, Republican Gerald Heikes and retired Petersburg teacher Dan J. Sullivan. Whether the similarly named candidate diverted votes or affected the outcome remains unproven. Chamberlain told Fox News Digital the alleged operation could constitute a federal felony if prosecutors establish that participants conspired to interfere with voters' constitutional rights. PELTOLA CAMPAIGN'S ALLEGED DAN SULLIVAN SPOILER PLOT TAKES NEW TURN AS DOJ FACES MAJOR LEGAL HURDLE "The basic concept is you're not allowed to conspire to injure or harm people's constitutional rights. And one of those rights is to vote for the candidate of your choice," Chamberlain said. "These people conspired to put a fake ‘Decoy Dan’ Sullivan on the ballot in order to trick people who were going into the ballot box intending to vote for the incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan," he alleged. "There's a lot of good precedent on this that suggests that's a crime and a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison." Chamberlain cited historical cases involving ballot manipulation, while acknowledging that the precise circumstances of recruiting a same-name candidate have not previously been addressed in an identical case. "Nothing exactly like this has happened before in the sense of recruiting a same-name candidate to trick people in the ballot box," he said, adding that a lot of slanted electoral messaging is not illegal. ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME "If you want to pretend that another Republican is better than the current incumbent or pretend that the incumbent's not running and then persuade someone to vote for that candidate, that's not a ‘conspiracy against rights’ because the right to vote for the candidate of your choice has not been impinged upon," he said. "It's the fact that when you're conspiring to put two people with the exact same name on the ballot to trick people who are going in there intending to vote for the incumbent and get them to vote for somebody else by deception." Meanwhile, former state Rep. David Eastman, a Republican from the Matanuska-Susitna Valley, told Fox News Digital by phone from Wasilla that he was approached by an operative under what he later surmised were false pretenses to recruit him into the race. Eastman said he also received several "fake mailers" suggesting "Decoy Dan" Sullivan was the real or only Sullivan in the race. The mailers, shared with Fox News Digital, are framed in a "meet the candidates" format and do omit Senator Sullivan. Eastman told Fox News Digital he was approached in the Mat-Su by an operative he later identified in a blog post as Jerid Kurtz, who was named in the New York Times report. Eastman said the operative claimed to represent conservative donors and encouraged him to run for Senate. "He approached me through a constituent. I sat down with him in April here in Wasilla," Eastman said. "He pretended to represent conservative donors and was looking for conservative candidates to run for federal office; none of which was true," Eastman added. Eastman alleged Kurtz "pretended" to represent conservative donors and used a false name, but said the operative never mentioned either Sullivan or disclosed an intention to confuse voters during their meeting. Fox News Digital reached out to the DSCC, Peltola’s campaign and Wingspan Strategies — where Kurtz is named in congressional documents as a co-owner — for comment. Dan J. Sullivan reportedly "vanished" as investigators began knocking on doors in his remote community, according to the Wall Street Journal. The allegations come as federal investigators examine whether Democratic political operatives improperly recruited Dan J. Sullivan in an effort to confuse voters who intended to support Senator Sullivan. The controversy has also reached Capitol Hill. In an October 29 letter, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., requested that Kurtz appear for an in-person transcribed interview on November 6 concerning allegations that operatives associated with Mary Peltola's campaign sought to recruit similarly named candidates to confuse voters. "As a Democrat operative who was allegedly tasked with assisting in this effort, you have information that will assist the Committee's investigation," Comer wrote. "If you do not voluntarily appear for the interview, we will be forced to evaluate the use of compulsory process," he warned. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Eastman said Kurtz did not mention either Sullivan or disclose an effort to confuse voters during their April meeting. He nevertheless questioned the operative's intentions after subsequent reporting connected Kurtz to the alleged candidate recruitment effort. articles.title: Why did Republicans lose the midterms?
articles.summary: Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong, and a brewing blame-game that's exp...
articles.body:
Washington — Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong and a brewing blame game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.

From House and Senate races to governors' mansions, Republicans saw striking losses, both in battlegrounds and in places where the party saw significant support just two years ago. The victories dramatically shifted the balance of power in Washington, delivering Democrats a sizable majority in the House far beyond what was expected heading into Election Day, as well as a Senate majority larger than what the GOP has enjoyed for the last two years.

As Republicans process the results, including some GOP officials who have ambitions of their own in 2028, they're offering frank assessments of the shortcomings — and laying the groundwork for where the party heads next.

Throughout the country, as Republicans tried to rally support around their accomplishments over the last two years, the president's war in Iran loomed large. And in this week's elections, its impact on the economy and prices appeared to overshadow most everything else.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vice President JD Vance said in a candid post on social media that was among the first efforts from a top Republican to unpack the party's losses.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay," said Vance, who is widely seen as a possible presidential contender in 2028. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

Asked about the comments, President Trump told reporters that it's "largely true" that Republicans lost the House and Senate because war led to higher energy prices, agreeing with Vance. But he also argued that the war has been worthwhile.

"If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," Mr. Trump said.

Early in the war, Mr. Trump acknowledged that the vice president was "philosophically, a little bit different than me," and was "less enthusiastic about going" into Iran. Still, Vance has largely stood by Mr. Trump on Iran.

GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who called the midterms a "Watergate-level repudiation," also cited the war, saying, "the Iran war has dragged on too long."

"It should have been brief, decisive, and over — it needs to end," said Cruz, who has vocally supported the war .

But Cruz pointed more broadly to the war's impact on prices, citing gas and diesel, along with the impacts of the president's trade policy, saying, "Tariffs have made everything too expensive."

Former Vice President Mike Pence also criticized Republicans' handling of the Iran war, but from the opposite direction , writing that the "unfinished war against Iran became an albatross around the necks of Republicans because Washington stopped short and pursued appeasement rather than allowing our troops to finish off the threat posed by the Iranian regime, once and for all."

More so than the war in Iran, voters nationally said cost of living was a major factor in their vote, according to CBS News exit polls .

Cruz said many GOP candidates this cycle seemed "like they didn't understand or they didn't care" about the cost of living. He said there's a "very real economic disconnect: Our K-shaped economy is a yawning divide," referring to the idea that some Americans' fortunes are on the upswing while others are pointing downward .

The Texas Republican cited Elon Musk becoming the world's first trillionaire, while at the same time, millions of Americans struggled to feed their families. And as data centers were constructed and the wealthiest people became even wealthier, he said Americans saw their electricity bills go up significantly in recent years.

"Understandably, people were pissed off," he said. "And elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain."

Democrats hammered Republicans over the cost of living, as economic populism became a key tenet of the cycle, while some candidates, like James Talarico in Texas, billed the fight as top-versus-bottom, rather than left-versus-right. Texas Republicans suffered one of the most striking routs of the midterms: Starting next year, Cruz will be one of the only Republican statewide elected officials in a state that was once viewed as almost imperviously red.

GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, whose seat Talarico will take in the new year after Cornyn lost his primary to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lamented that after voters trusted Mr. Trump and the GOP to "protect their pocketbooks" in the 2024 elections, the president "misread his mandate."

"Voters wanted to retool our trading relationships, but got arbitrary 'Liberation Day' tariffs that raised prices without creating incentives for long-term reshoring," Cornyn wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed. "Voters wanted secure borders and peaceful streets, but got hyperaggressive immigration enforcement. The Iran conflict came with no attempt to persuade the public. And Mr. Trump signaled disconnection by focusing on sideshows like swimming-pool liners in the Reflecting Pool."

Cornyn added, "Americans elected the Donald Trump who put on the apron of the Golden Arches and got a plan for a Triumphal Arch instead."

Cornyn, who was formerly the No. 2 Senate Republican, also pointed to how corruption surged to a top issue for voters, "thanks to flawed midterm candidates and a parade of unsavory headlines out of Washington."

Democrats like Talarico worked hard to tie corruption to cost-of-living concerns expressed widely. And roughly nine in 10 voters nationally said government corruption was a major factor in their vote.

"Voters won't trust Republicans to cut fraud and scams out of government programs until we cut them out of our own ranks," Cornyn wrote. "Party leaders have to stop excusing the inexcusable and police our side of the aisle — or voters will continue to police it for us."

Beyond the cost-of-living concerns, some Republicans also pointed to an over-emphasis on culture war issues.

Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the midterm outcomes as "close to an extension-level event for Republicans as we have seen probably in the last hundred years," said he knew Republicans were in trouble when he saw they were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ads centering transgender issues.

"That was not the issue motivating voters, and it was kind of like an attempt to just scare Republicans to vote," DeSantis said at a news conference.

By late October, more than $180 million had been spent on ads that centered transgender-related attacks against Democrats, according to the Associated Press, reminiscent of the "Kamala is for they/them, Trump is for you" ads that blanketed the airwaves in the 2024 presidential election.

DeSantis — who has staked out conservative positions on transgender issues — argued the issue is no longer as potent, saying: "Four years ago, we were in the peak-woke era." But now, he argued, "the issues are different."

"Republicans, it seemed like — in some of the ads I was seeing, with how much money they were spending — they really were fighting yesterday's battles," he said.

As Republicans turned their attention to transgender and other culture-war issues, Democrats didn't give the attacks traction, shifting the focus at nearly every turn to affordability concerns. Some moderate Democrats in battleground states also voiced opposition to transgender athletes' participation in girls' sports, which may have neutralized some attacks.

But DeSantis also argued the election wasn't the result of voters having positive views of Democrats — exit polling shows voters had unfavorable opinions of both parties, though Republicans' favorability (40%) was lower than Democrats' (47%).

Instead, DeSantis said, it was a "rejection of Republicans in Washington." And that rebuke wasn't only aimed at the president, he argued, but also the GOP-controlled Congress, as voters became "frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate."

"So it's really both sides of Pennsylvania Avenue," DeSantis said. "It's not just one."

articles.title: DeSantis nukes ‘tech guy’ Vivek after Ohio drubbing: ‘Not in tune’ with blue-collar voters
articles.summary: Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis says Vivek Ramaswamy wasn't "in tune" with Ohio's blue-collar voters, citing his tech background and H-1B stance.
articles.body: Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis blasted failed Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and his GOP handlers, arguing on a podcast that he wasn't "in tune" with the working-class people of the state. Biotech entrepreneur Ramaswamy lost his scandal-plagued race to Democratic candidate Amy Acton by 7.9 percentage points. Despite President Donald Trump’s endorsement and guidance from Vice President JD Vance’s top advisers, Ramaswamy lost amid a "blue wave" that produced major Democratic upsets across the country. The midterm elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's presidency. But DeSantis, who ran for president in 2024 and is term-limited after 2026, shared on the Sage Steele Show that Ramaswamy bore some responsibility for his loss. "I don't know why they would have pushed him to be the candidate there. Oh, my mom's from Youngstown. Ohio is a working class state, very blue collar. You know Vivek, he's like a tech guy," DeSantis said. RAMASWAMY OUTLINES KEY CONTRASTS WITH DEM OPPONENT LESS THAN 100 DAYS OUT FROM KEY GUBERNATORIAL ELECTION Ramaswamy, who previously ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024, is the founder of biotech company Roivant Sciences and anti-ESG investment firm Strive Asset Management. He also briefly co-led President Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency with Elon Musk. He was warmly embraced by Trump, who endorsed him the same day Ramaswamy announced his candidacy. Trump had previously encouraged Ramaswamy to consider seeking Vance’s former Senate seat. Ramaswamy and Vance have known each other since their time at Yale Law School. DeSantis criticized Ramaswamy’s support for a merit-based H-1B visa system, arguing that it likely further distanced him from Ohio’s blue-collar voters. Ramaswamy had said the current lottery-based system should be "gutted." 'He wants to bring in foreign workers on visas. That is not the type of person that's going to sell." DeSantis said. Ramaswamy's own companies have used the H-1B program, with Roivant Sciences having 29 H-1B applications approved between 2018 and 2023. Meanwhile, Strive Asset Management, the investment firm he co-founded, moved its headquarters from Columbus to Dallas in 2025, months before Ramaswamy launched his campaign for Ohio governor. Ramaswamy said he was no longer involved in the company’s operations, but remained a major shareholder. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS "And I know he shot himself in the foot," DeSantis said. "I know he did a lot of other stuff to make it a real landslide against him. But even with that, it's like you know you got to meet the voters where they are on some of this stuff," DeSantis said. "I think we would have done better in Ohio had we had a candidate that was more representative or more in tune with the interests of kind of these blue collar people that make the backbone of Ohio." Just weeks before the election, Ramaswamy’s campaign drew bipartisan outrage for using Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton’s estranged mother in an attack ad that called the Democratic candidate a "liar" and disputed her account of childhood poverty and homelessness. The ad omitted that Acton had not seen or spoken to her mother since age 12, when her stepfather was arrested on charges of raping her. He pleaded not guilty but fled the area before trial, and court records show authorities continued seeking his arrest for years. Acton’s brother has said their mother remained married to him until his death in 2004. Ramaswamy's loss, alongside Republican U.S. Senate candidate Jon Husted's loss to Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown by 4.9 percentage points, came just two years after Trump won the state by 11.2 percentage points. DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED In addition to criticizing Ramaswamy, DeSantis took aim at Congress, saying Republicans are now on the "defensive" and faulting lawmakers for failing to codify Trump’s executive orders into law. "Last night's elections did not only kneecap the last two years of the Trump administration, it basically ensures the four years after that are going to either be Democrat years where they have a trifecta or where you have a Republican president that is hemmed in and limited," DeSantis said. DeSantis also pushed back against any 2028 speculation. articles.title: Generation Z and young voters help redefine US politics after midterms
articles.summary: Melat Kiros becomes the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress, embodying a new era of political representation.
articles.body:
The outcome of the 2026 US midterm elections has marked a historic shift in American politics, with diverse candidates winning office and the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress.

Of the 117 Generation Z candidates who ran for Congress this year, 24 won their primaries and made it to Tuesday’s ballot, according to the organisation Future Caucus.

Among them was Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old Ethiopian-born democratic socialist from Colorado, who became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

Kiros, a lawyer turned doctoral student, won a stunning primary victory earlier this year, with the first-time candidate beating 30-year incumbent Representative Diana DeGette in the Denver-area seat.

After winning the primary, she told supporters that she was taking the fight to “Donald Trump and the oligarchy”, abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), passing Medicare for All and ending the “genocide in Palestine”.

She joins Representative Maxwell Frost of Florida, who became the first Gen Z member of the House in 2022.

Young people voted overwhelmingly for Democrats, according to an Associated Press news agency voter poll.

After relatively high support for Trump in the 2024 election, young voters snapped back towards the Democratic Party in this year’s midterms.

The AP Voter Poll showed about seven in 10 voters under 30 nationally said they supported the Democratic candidate in their local US House race, while about three in 10 said they voted for the Republican. That was a dramatic shift from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Kamala Harris.

Most first-time midterm voters, who skew younger, also supported the Democratic candidate.

Both young voters and first-time voters made up a fairly small share of the electorate. Only about one in 10 voters in the 2026 national electorate are under 30, for instance, which limited the impact of the shift.

But young voters’ displeasure with the country and its leadership was clear. About half of young voters said they were “angry” about the way things were going in the country, compared with only about one-third of voters aged 65 and older. And about six in 10 voters under 30 said one reason for their vote for the US House was to express opposition to Trump, compared with about half of voters aged 30-44 and about four in 10 voters aged 45 and older.

Young voters shifted towards the Democrats in each of the Senate races where the Democratic Party picked up a seat, including in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina.

articles.title: How the Mississippi Senate race between Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith got so close — and what happens next
articles.summary: Ballots are still being counted, but Colom's lead has grown by more than 1,500 votes since Election Day.
articles.body:
Mississippi is one of the reddest states in America, so this year's U.S. Senate race between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and her Democratic challenger Scott Colom wasn't supposed to be especially close.

As of Thursday afternoon, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by a mere 1,724 votes, according to the Associated Press. That's just 0.19% of all ballots cast. As a result, the AP has yet to call the contest, even though 96% of the vote is in.

Along with Alaska — which also remains too close to call — the outcome in Mississippi will determine whether Democrats can expand their new Senate majority beyond its current size (54 seats) by flipping even more red states than they already have .

But Alaska was supposed to be a toss-up . Mississippi wasn't really on the national radar. President Trump won the state by 23 percentage points in 2024 — his third straight win there. Looking ahead to the 2026 Senate race, analysts said it was a "likely Republican" hold . Barely anyone bothered to poll it .

Yet, here we are, with Colom edging Hyde-Smith as officials tally the final votes. How did the Mississippi Senate race get so close — and what happens next?

Colom, 43, was born in Columbus, Miss., to two lawyers who also participated in politics. In 1987, his father, Wilbur, ran for state treasurer as a Republican; his mother, Dorothy, served as the first Black Chancery Court judge in their home district. Colom earned his JD from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and went on to serve as the first Black justice court judge in Lowndes County, Miss., before becoming the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus.

In 2015, Colom defeated a nearly 30-year incumbent to become the first Black district attorney elected in a majority-white voting district in Mississippi history. He has since prosecuted a number of high-profile murder and sexual assault cases.

In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi. Leading Magnolia State Republicans — including Sen. Roger Wicker and former Govs. Phil Bryant and Haley Barbour — backed Colom's nomination.

"I have known two generations of the Colom family for over 20 years and believe Scott Colom possesses the discernment to be a fair and exemplary judge," Bryant told the New York Times .

But Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination in the Senate, citing support his 2015 campaign received from a political action committee funded by George Soros and claiming that he favored allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls' and women's sports. The White House characterized Hyde-Smith's concerns as " spurious ."

In a letter to Hyde-Smith urging her to reconsider, Colom confirmed that he had signed a letter with other prosecutors condemning efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care for transgender people, but insisted that their joint statement "did not comment on legislation specifically related to participation in athletics." Colom also said he had not known about Soros's contributions to the Mississippi Safety and Justice PAC "until I read about them in my hometown paper."

Colom's unsuccessful nomination was returned to Biden on Jan. 3, 2024. In September 2025, Colom announced his U.S. Senate candidacy.

Hyde-Smith, 67, is a former lobbyist and state legislator who was serving as Mississippi's agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2018 following the resignation of Republican Sen. Thad Cochran. She won a 2018 special election and a 2020 full-term election, and she has served in the Senate ever since.

There were signs before Tuesday that Hyde-Smith might be vulnerable to "voter apathy," as one Mississippi State University political science professor recently put it . Sen. Wicker won reelection in 2024 by 25 points; Hyde-Smith's margin of victory in 2020 was less than half that. And while the only polls made public this cycle showed Hyde-Smith ahead , her leads were stuck in the single digits — no survey put her support above 50%. One April Democratic poll showed Hyde-Smith trailing a hypothetical "someone else" 33% to 53%.

Regardless, Hyde-Smith seemed content to coast to reelection, barely bothering to appear on the campaign trail. But Colom didn't have that luxury — and when he cut a viral campaign ad about beef prices in mid-October, the tide started to turn.

Asked earlier this year about soaring costs, including the price of beef, Hyde-Smith told local TV station WLOX that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys," but "you have so many proteins to choose from."

In the final weeks of the campaign, Colom seized on Hyde-Smith's remark about "proteins" to mock her with a spot featuring incredulous Mississippians grilling burgers, dining out and shopping for groceries — and saying they'd rather "pick another senator instead" (along with other, more colorful language). The video has since racked up nearly 14 million views on Colom's X account .

When the ad took off, national Democrats sprang into action. The Senate Majority PAC poured $2.2 million into the race; Senate Democrats' campaign arm contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia rushed to Mississippi to rally with Colom. In response, Republicans were forced to play defense, sending Trump to Mississippi in the final days of the campaign (along with cash infusions of their own).

In the end, it wasn't enough to give Hyde-Smith a decisive victory on Election Day. When Trump came to Mississippi, Colom went to his event to talk to rally-goers about health care, grocery bills and gas prices.

"I got the best message ever for Republican voters in Mississippi," he told CNN afterward. "I'm going to get you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised lower grocery prices on Day One. That's what I will fight for. You were promised no more endless wars. That's what I will fight for. You were promised the full and transparent release of the Epstein files. That's what I will fight for."

According to preliminary New York Times estimates , Colom performed 19 points better among white Mississippi voters than Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee. He won new voters — that is, those who didn't vote in 2024 — by 25 points.

The contest between Colom and Hyde-Smith hasn't been called yet because officials are waiting on two remaining batches of ballots.

The first batch comes from 11 counties that have yet to report 10% or more of their returns. The other batch contains affidavit ballots, which were generally cast by people who did not present an acceptable photo ID at the polls or who had been marked as inactive on voter rolls.

County clerks in Mississippi have 10 days — in this case, until Nov. 13 — to certify the election.

Five of the counties with outstanding ballots have favored Colom, including Hinds County (the most populous in the state). Five have favored Hyde-Smith. One is a toss-up. Any mail ballots from those counties must arrive by Tuesday, Nov. 10, in order to count.

As for the affidavit ballots, voters need to validate them with an acceptable ID by the same day: Nov. 10. The Colom campaign has said that roughly 10,000 to 15,000 affidavit ballots were cast this year.

Colom's team believes his lead will expand once those affidavit ballots are counted. (It has already grown by more than 1,500 votes since Election Day.) Ahead of Mississippi's March primaries, incorrect Experian information mistakenly led to the inactivation of legitimate voters — and inactivations have more than doubled in some jurisdictions since then. Discrepancies caused confusion and long lines at polling places on Tuesday, forcing affected voters to cast affidavit ballots.

"We are going to make sure every single vote has been counted, and I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat," Colom wrote on X on Wednesday morning . He added on Thursday that "my campaign, alongside the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] and Elias Law Group, Lisa Ross, and our great team of local attorneys, are leading the effort to ensure every eligible voter is heard."

Hyde-Smith also expressed confidence on Election Night. "We still don't have all the votes in, so we're not calling all of it tonight, but we're in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator," she told supporters at the time.

On Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party chairman Mike Hurst estimated that about 20,000 ballots had not been counted yet. "We are enthusiastic about these outstanding ballots because a number of these, a significant number of these, we believe, are in and remain in Republican-leaning districts, precincts and counties throughout the state," Hurst told reporters.

Mississippi is the only state in the country without a recount law. But if the margin is still razor-close next week, Colom or Hyde-Smith could challenge certain ballots in court. That would likely happen after certification on Nov. 13.

Lawyers for Hyde-Smith and her campaign have formally written to Mississippi state officials to demand "the immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation of all affidavit ballots," according to the New York Times — a signal that they may pursue litigation if those ballots put Colom over the top.

articles.title: Sizing up the blue wave: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Democrats are on track for the second-biggest House popular vote edge in the last 50 years. This will also be the largest midterm margin for one party since 1974.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Scott Bland takes stock of the scope of Democrats’ gains in the House. Plus, Alexandra Marquez examines how the party’s midterm success could affect the next presidential contest. — Adam Wollner Sizing up the blue wave Analysis by Scott Bland Democrats’ performance in Tuesday’s election was obviously big — you can’t reach an estimated 259 House seats without sizable national margins. A historical look shows just how massive the results were, too. Democrats are on track for the second-biggest House popular vote edge in the last 50 years. This will also be the largest midterm margin for one party since 1974, when the country punished the Republican Party in the first election after Richard Nixon resigned following the Watergate scandal. With more votes still left to count, especially in Democratic-leaning California, House Democratic candidates have captured 55.3% of the national vote, compared to 43.3% for Republicans. That’s an 12-point margin — more than Democrats in 2008 (10.5 points) or 2018 (8.6 points) and more than Republicans in their wave years of 1994 (6.8 points), 2010 (6.6 points) and 2014 (5.8 points). Ben Kamisar, Sarah Sternhagen and Stephen Pettigrew zeroed in on the shifts in the House races that were rated as “battleground districts” by NBC News’ Decision Desk before the election.The average “battleground” district’s margin moved almost 17 percentage points toward Democrats when compared to the 2024 presidential margin there, according to a review of the election results in 21 of the 28 battlegrounds where at least 95% of the expected vote is in. The two biggest swings came in South Texas, where a dramatic Democratic improvement among Latino voters helped power massive congressional victories. Newly elected Democrats could become 2028 presidential power brokers By Alexandra Marquez The 2026 midterm elections are not quite over, but the 2028 presidential race may soon get underway. And with sweeping victories for Democrats in races across the country Tuesday night, voters in states with early Democratic presidential primaries also elected a new class of kingmakers. New Democratic governors or senators will soon take over in five of the six states that will lead the party’s presidential primary calendar in two years. Those leaders’ endorsements could be major prizes for candidates and signals for voters, especially in states that elected Democrats statewide for the first time in decades. The prime example is South Carolina, where Annie Andrews became the first Democrat elected to the Senate there since 1998. In August, the Democratic National Committee voted to make South Carolina the first state on its presidential primary calendar in 2028. Historically, when the state was in the third spot on the calendar, Democratic Rep. James Clyburn’s backing was known to sway primaries. He is credited with propelling President Joe Biden’s campaign to victory in 2020. Now, Andrews could join Clyburn as a statewide voice for Democratic voters looking to nominate a future president. “I mentioned it to Annie last night. I said, ‘You know, you’re going to be extremely popular with all the 2028 folks,’” Jamie Harrison, former chair of the Democratic National Committee and the South Carolina Democratic Party, told NBC News on Wednesday. “She just started laughing. But she will be.” Read more → 🗳️Related: Rep. Ro Khanna allies launch a draft campaign for the 2028 presidential race, by Jonathan Allen That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
