articles.title: Republicans have control of Congress for 2 more months. Here’s what they hope to get done.
articles.summary: A looming shutdown, military funding and a potential impeachment vote are just some of the high-stakes items on the GOP’s agenda before Democrats take over.
articles.body:
Republicans on Capitol Hill are on the clock. They have less than two months left in power before the new, Democrat-led Congress is sworn in and their window of unified control in Washington, D.C., comes to an end. Even as the votes are still being counted, GOP leaders have been putting together plans for what they hope to accomplish before they lose power.

"Our job is nowhere close to being finished yet," House Speaker Mike Johnson reportedly told attendees at a watch party Tuesday night as Democratic victories piled up.

The period between the November election and the day in early January when new lawmakers are sworn in, often called the "lame duck" session, can be quite productive as lawmakers move with urgency to get things done while they still can. Some of the most important actions taken by Congress in modern history — the legislative response to the Watergate scandal, the Clinton impeachment, the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and several Supreme Court confirmations — all happened during various lame duck windows.

Republicans will have a long list of priorities when Congress reconvenes on Monday, but there are also plenty of potential hurdles that could hinder their progress. Here's a look at what congressional Republicans want to do and some of the possible curveballs that could derail their plans.

Congress will have two "must-pass" items on its agenda when it gets back to work next week: avoiding another government shutdown and passing an annual defense policy bill. Leaders from both parties say they want to get both bills done, but disagreement on the specifics could make for a bumpy and time-consuming process.

The government will shut down again on Dec. 12 if Congress doesn't pass a funding bill to keep it open. After enduring the two longest shutdowns in history over the past two years, neither party appears eager to let another one happen. The big point of disagreement could be timing. Republican leaders are reportedly eyeing a bill that would lock in current spending levels for a full year, but Democrats have an incentive to advocate for a short-term bill that sets them up to enact their own spending priorities once they're in full control of Congress.

Negotiations over the defense budget could be even thornier. The Trump administration has asked Congress for $1.5 trillion in military funding for 2027. Democrats have balked at that number, demanding that the price tag be reduced by hundreds of billions of dollars. Reports suggest that the administration may be open to shrinking its budget request, but landing on a final number that both parties and the president can agree on could prove challenging — particularly if the White House insists on including more funding for the war with Iran.

"I don't know what [Trump's] going to want. I don't know how we're going to figure out the money. So no, I don't have easy answers to that," Rep. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, told Politico on Wednesday.

Even if both bills eventually get passed, drawn-out negotiations could eat up precious time and leave little room for Congress to do much else before the end of the year.

In the wake of Tuesday's losses, some Republican lawmakers have begun advocating for their party to pass one last major budget bill jam-packed with GOP priorities. To do that, they'd need to use the same process they utilized to pass Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill, which creates a pathway to circumvent the Senate filibuster and approve legislation without any Democratic votes.

"It's time to wake up and smell the coffee," Trump adviser Jason Miller told GOP lawmakers on Wednesday. "You have one job. Get everything on President Trump's agenda through in the limited days we have."

Before the election, Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno told reporters that he would push for a "giant" spending package during the lame-duck session if the GOP lost both chambers of Congress.

Actually getting another Republican megabill passed could be a steep challenge. Negotiations over the massive list of complex provisions within the One Big Beautiful Bill took months and consumed big chunks of the congressional calendar.

Republicans may also have a numbers problem. Any bill they put forward would need near-unanimous support within their party in both chambers. That includes outgoing senators Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, who have been at odds with the president in the late stages of their time in Congress.

Republicans also have other, less ambitious priorities that could be at risk if they dedicate their time and energy to another huge party-line budget bill. One of those priorities is a bipartisan proposal to overhaul the permitting process for energy projects, which would make it easier to build both renewable and fossil fuel infrastructure. There's also a sweeping slate of reforms to college sports , a number of Trump-nominated judges awaiting confirmation , cryptocurrency legislation and more that could end up on the GOP's long to-do list.

One of the biggest questions looming over Washington, D.C., since Tuesday is whether any of the Supreme Court's conservative justices might retire during the lame-duck session. With Democrats pledging to prevent Trump from putting another "right-winger" on the court, this could be a conservative justice's last chance — potentially for years — to retire with the confidence that their replacement is likely to share their ideology.

Neither of the court's two oldest justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, has given any indication that they're considering stepping down — in fact, Alito has reportedly been unequivocal about his plans to stay on the bench. But if one of them did, Republicans would be heavily incentivized to put everything else on the back burner to rush the confirmation of their replacement before Democrats gain the power to block Trump's nominees for the rest of his presidency.

Republicans' calendar may also get scrambled by some of their own outgoing members. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has been a key voice behind the push for disclosures about the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein, has said he plans to force a second vote on the issue before he leaves Congress.

Massie has said he's also planning to introduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced heavy scrutiny for his role in carrying out the war in Iran. Tillis recently told CBS News that Hegseth faces a "reckoning" when Congress reconvenes next week.

It's unclear how much support Massie's impeachment effort has in the House, but even if it failed, it could consume valuable time Republican leaders would rather spend on other priorities. The same would be true of confirmation hearings for a new defense secretary if reports that Trump is considering firing Hegseth prove to be accurate.

articles.title: What will Democrats prioritize with control of Congress?
articles.summary: With two years left in office, Trump's veto power could present a challenge for the Democrats' congressional agenda.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January , their agenda will look much different than President Donald Trump and Republican's initiatives.

Affordability was top of mind for many voters during the midterm elections, and Democrats have floated several ideas for addressing the high cost of living. This includes reinstating some Obamacare tax credits, reversing some of the Medicaid cuts and voting to bring an end to the war in Iran .

Democrats have also floated AI legislation, pushing to include protections for people living in communities where data centers are built, ensuring they don't bear the costs. There may also be an attempt to repeal tariffs that Trump has put in place.

Trump in office 2 more years: What does that mean for Democrats' agenda?

Trump still has two years left in office, however, and his veto power could present a challenge for the Democrats' congressional agenda and their ability to pass legislation.

Still, Trump's veto can always be overridden, but that takes two-thirds of both chambers. That would require at least 290 members of the House and 67 in the Senate. Even if Democrats win most of the uncalled races, they'd still need significant Republican support in both chambers to override the veto.

Will Democrats hold the Trump administration accountable?

Democratic control of Congress also means that investigations and subpoenas are likely coming for several members of the Trump administration, including cabinet officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Both were subjects of impeachment investigations or inquiries prior to the midterm elections.

Still, the minority leader and likely Speaker of the House in 2027, Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said the House Democratic Caucus hasn't brought up impeachment, reiterating that Democrats' main focus is affordability.

NewsNation's Jeff Arnold and Sana Azem contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump wants his arch approved Thursday — and to immediately start work
articles.summary: President Donald Trump hopes to win approval Thursday for his planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch, which he calls a necessary addition to Washington. He may...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump hopes to win approval Thursday for his planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch, which he calls a necessary addition to Washington. He may end the day with work finally underway - or blocked by a federal judge.

The National Capital Planning Commission, which Trump has stocked with allies, on Thursday afternoon began reviewing final plans for the arch, proposed near Arlington National Cemetery. The commission is expected to approve the project - after extensive public testimony and debate - and administration officials say they could begin construction immediately.

The project's opponents have beseeched U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan to stop work before it starts. "The Court should not allow this lawless project to evade scrutiny," Brian Schwalb and Jay Jones, the attorneys general for D.C. and Virginia, wrote in a joint court filing Wednesday.

D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson, who sits on the National Capital Planning Commission, pressed Trump officials Thursday on their project plans, the president's claims that the arch would double as a "military complex" and the expected number of tourists.

"What is the purpose of this memorial?" Mendelson asked, noting that lawmakers a century ago envisioned a pair of columns symbolizing the nation's reunification after the Civil War - a different plan than what the administration is pursuing. He also warned that the project could hamper emergency evacuation from Washington.

Trump has spent more than a year touting his plan for the arch, which he says is needed to commemorate the nation's 250th anniversary. The monument would rise in Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout tucked inside Washington's boundaries. The current Congress has not authorized the project, and opponents argue it would violate multiple federal laws, overwhelm the site and wrongly overshadow the national military cemetery.

The Trump administration says building the arch will complete the century-old vision for the site that Congress had authorized. The president extolled the arch again Wednesday while touring another of his projects, a new White House ballroom, and touted his continued efforts to remake Washington.

The triumphal arch is "like the Arc de Triomphe, but better, more beautiful actually, much more beautiful," the president told reporters at the White House, invoking the Parisian arch that inspired his own.

More than 120 people have signed up to testify at Thursday's National Capital Planning Commission hearing. The initial speakers included four lawmakers who split on whether the arch should be approved, several Vietnam War veterans who said it would harm their experience of visiting the military cemetery, and advocacy groups that urged Trump to stop the project.

Many called the planned structure and site unsuitable. The representative of an architects association criticized Trump's design, and the head of the D.C. Preservation League said the towering structure would violate a federal law limiting the height of new buildings.

"This commission's own 2001 Memorials and Museums Master Plan rules out Memorial Circle for a memorial ," Bryan Clark Green, an architectural historian, told the panel.

Mark Paoletta, a White House official who chairs the commission, said Thursday that he plans to approve the project, praising Trump's "historic vision" and saying the project would provide "a generational security opportunity" to protect the capital.

The empty space at Memorial Circle "dishonors our veterans and leaves a key monumental gateway to Arlington that Congress authorized uncompleted," Paoletta added. "This is a national disgrace."

Trump last month added more political appointees to the commission, including the Interior Department's Kevin Lilly and the Pentagon's Ricky Buria. Six of the panel's 12 seats are controlled by Trump, and two more are held by his GOP congressional allies, who have swiftly approved the president's past projects. Lilly, a veteran, said Thursday that he supported the arch because it honored America's ideals and military service.

GOP Reps. Andrew Clyde (Georgia) and Brian Mast (Florida) joined the hearing to argue that the arch should move forward. Both men are military veterans, and the Trump administration has contended that the arch would honor veterans rather than impose on the cemetery.

Democratic Reps. Jared Huffman (California) and Don Beyer (Virginia) called the project illegal, portrayed it as a monument to Trump and said the administration needed to submit the plans to Congress for approval.

Huffman's comments drew a response from Paoletta, and the two men argued for several minutes about the intent for Memorial Circle and the nearby Arlington Memorial Bridge. Paoletta said the Democratic congressman was wrongly characterizing the scope of the original, century-old construction plan, citing correspondence from long-ago officials.

"This is tortured stuff," Huffman told Paoletta. "Why don't you take your shot with Judge Chutkan on this one? … I feel pretty good about where that's going to come down."

Chutkan, who is weighing two lawsuits against the arch, has ordered the Trump administration to provide immediate updates about the project's status and construction plans. She has also voiced skepticism of Trump's national security arguments for the project, saying officials have failed to provide evidence for that purpose and suggesting that the administration should not invoke national security as a "talismanic" justification for controversial projects.

"What is the harm of waiting?" Chutkan asked a DOJ official last Friday, as she heard dueling arguments from the administration and lawyers for Vietnam veterans and a historic preservationist. "What is the rush to put this arch up?"

The D.C. government and state of Virginia sued the next day, contending that the project would impede traffic, interfere with emergency evacuation planning and cause other local disruptions. Trump officials have argued that the alleged harms are too speculative and that the challenge should be thrown out.

The Trump administration has closely guarded its plans for some of Trump's projects, and has declined to release the names of contractors teed up to work on the arch or how it will be paid for.

A vehicle bearing the logo of a division of Grunley Construction, a local firm that has worked on the White House's Eisenhower Executive Office Building and other government buildings, was seen at the site on Tuesday according to a photograph posted by independent journalist Andrew Leyden.

The Interior Department, which is managing the arch project, and Grunley Construction did not respond to requests for comment about whether the company is involved in the project. The Justice Department late Wednesday night said in a court filing that Grunley Construction "may be - but is not necessarily" preparing for work on the project.

Trump officials have told Chutkan that contractors are prepared to fence off Memorial Circle and begin staging supplies nearby as soon as the arch is approved by the National Capital Planning Commission and the Interior Department formally authorizes the project shortly afterward.

D.C. and Virginia leaders say work should be paused now.

"The District and Virginia are plainly harmed by the construction of a massive Arch that will clog traffic on a major thoroughfare, undermine emergency preparedness, inflict environmental damage, and subvert the region's historic plan," Schwalb and Jones wrote in their filing. "Those irreparable injuries will begin to accrue the moment construction begins."

articles.title: Some Democratic Senate candidates would have won even if nobody voted for them on Election Day
articles.summary: How dominant were Democrats in the 2026 election? They could have won some marquee races even if literally none of their voters showed up on Election Day.
articles.body:
How dominant were Democrats in the 2026 election?

So dominant that they could have won some marquee races even if literally none of their voters showed up on Election Day.

That was true in Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas. And it could also be true of the Arizona governor's race.

In each one, more voters voted for the Democrat via early voting and absentee and/or mail voting than voted in total for the Republican — including all methods of voting. In each race, the Democrat appears to have won by 10 or more percentage points.

In Georgia, returns from the secretary of state show Sen. Jon Ossoff getting about 1,772,000 votes from early and absentee voting, compared to about 1,712,000 total votes for his opponent, GOP Rep. Mike Collins.

Ossoff's current lead stands at 18 points.

In Texas, data from the secretary of state shows Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico got 4.4 million early votes, compared to 4.25 million total votes for GOP state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Talarico surprised many by winning his race by double digits — in a state where Democrats hadn't won a statewide office since 1994.

In North Carolina, data from the State Board of Elections shows Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper receiving about 1,728,000 early in-person votes, compared to about 1,643,000 votes total for Republican Michael Whatley.

Cooper didn't even need absentee votes to beat Whatley. His early vote total trumped Whatley's total from early, absentee and Election Day voting. President Donald Trump came to the state repeatedly to try to help Whatley, and Cooper is currently winning by 20 points. He is the first Democrat North Carolina has elected to the Senate since 2008.

The stats reinforce just how crucial the early vote is to Democrats, in particular. Democratic voters remained significantly more likely to vote early than Republicans in these midterms.

In Texas, Talarico is currently getting more than 80% of his vote total from early votes. And in North Carolina, Cooper is getting 73% of his votes outside of Election Day voting.

The early vote dominance could also be the case in a governor's race in another swing state: Arizona.

There, the latest results show Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs getting more than 1 million early votes, compared to 960,000 total votes for Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Hobbs currently leads in her reelection race by 11 points.

Those numbers could shift, though, as the state has counted an estimated 86% of its vote.

The numbers are particularly striking given all of these races were once considered competitive. Three of them are in presidential swing states, while Texas has long been a red state.

And, if nothing else, the stats reinforce just how much US elections are now conducted outside of Election Day — and how parties could have major races in difficult states like these locked up before the regular polls even open.

articles.title: Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayor over incumbent Karen Bass
articles.summary: The results mean America's two most populous cities - New York and Los Angeles - will be led by democratic socialists.
articles.body:
Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.

Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.

Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.

Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.

Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."

"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".

She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.

The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.

The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.

Raman entered the race as a long-shot candidate but slowly shored up support, especially from younger voters, before besting reality star Spencer Pratt in the primary race earlier this year.

Raman's win over Bass has all the appearances of echoing voter sentiment across the US as part of sweeping Democratic wins, including in deep-Republican country that hadn't seen liberal leaders in decades.

Washington DC also elected democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George as its new mayor, furthering progressive leadership in another major US city.

US President Donald Trump was asked at the White House about the wins by politicians on the left flank of the Democratic Party and said, "If you go by history, it's going to be a disaster".

Such candidates have become a focal point of attacks by Republicans.

Bass had been a prominent member of Congress before becoming LA's first black mayor. Her roots are closely tied to LA and its history, even working as a community organiser during the violent 1992 riots over police brutality in the beating of Rodney King, who was black.

articles.title: Midterms 2026 election results and latest updates: Mississippi votes still being counted in Senate nail-biter after Democrats take control of Congress
articles.summary: As Democrats took a victory lap, President Trump distanced himself from a dismal GOP showing as the White House was left to reckon with a historic rout.
articles.body: Democrats continue to celebrate one of the most lopsided midterm election victories in modern U.S. history, routing their Republican rivals to gain control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country.In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats and now hold 54 to the Republican Party's 44. Two seats — nail-biting contests in Alaska and Mississippi — remain undeclared.To do so, Democrats won a series of key battleground contests. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in one of the most closely watched races of the midterms. James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the Lone Star State since 1988. Annie Andrews beat Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina to flip a Senate seat. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson defeated incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, putting an end to her three-decade tenure. Sen. Jon Ossoff comfortably won reelection in Georgia. Other Senate seats to flip to the Democratic Party included Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas.In the House, Democrats held 253 House seats to the GOP's 155 as of 6:30 p.m. ET Thursday, comfortably passing the majority threshold of 218, with 27 races still to be called. The latest estimates show that the party is on track to win its largest majority since 2008. And there are still seats it could flip, including Colorado's Fourth District, which is held by Republican incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert, a staunch Trump ally, whose race against Democrat Eileen Laubacher remains tight.There were also 36 gubernatorial races, mayoral contests and numerous ballot measures — and plenty of firsts. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history, while Democrat Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor-elect. El-Sayed will be America's first Muslim senator.At the White House, President Trump signaled he would work with Democrats during his remaining two years in office but said he wouldn't hesitate to use his veto power. The president also acknowledged Wednesday that the Iran war contributed to Republican losses, but defended his decision to pursue the conflict. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said, adding: "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."Vice President JD Vance had earlier blamed the scale of GOP losses on the war with Iran."The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," he wrote in a post on X. "The reason we lost is the war."
